To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of a CO(2) tunable laser to detect and identify explosives in the mid-wave infrared spectral region at distances of up the 150 m is feasible.
we have developed a novel, noncontact, nondestructive, and noninvasive technique for standoff detection of explosive substances.
we have developed a technique for detecting and identifying trace quantities of explosives in the presence of a large number of background materials at distances up to 500 meters.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel, highly sensitive, and selective methods for the detection and identification of explosive materials in the field and in the laboratory.
the detection of explosive materials in a standoff mode at distances approaching 1000 m and the detection of explosive residue at short distances, on the order of a few meters.
developing and demonstrating a new technique for standoff detection of explosives.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the detection sensitivity of explosives at standoff distance is a function of the target material, the detector used for measuring the blackbody radiation, the laser wavelength, the laser pulse duration, and the pulse repetition rate.
the detection and identification of explosives at long range is possible with a high degree of confidence and selectivity.

the technique is sensitive to trace amounts of explosives and that, with the availability and development of high power, mid-wave infrared and/or long-wave infrared quantum-cascade lasers, the detection sensitivity and range can be improved significantly.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the technology is mature for standoff detection at 150 m and is in a development stage for detection at 1 km.
this technology is capable of detecting and identifying explosives at a standoff distance of up to 1 km with high sensitivity (approximately 1 ng) and high selectivities (approximately 1 ppm).

we have demonstrated the capability to detect and identify trace quantities of explosives from a distance of 150 m. The detection sensitivity is comparable to that obtained with conventional standoff detection systems, such as those based on infrared absorption and laser-induced fluorescence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the technique can be applied at distances of up 1000 m, and the detection sensitivity is limited only by the power of the available lasers and the detector sensitivity.

the use of a CO(2) or quantum cascade laser for remote detection of explosives in the mid-wave infrared or long-wave infrared regions of the electromagnetic spectrum, respectively, can lead to significant improvement in detection sensitivity over the use of broadband sources.
it demonstrates the feasibility of detecting trace quantities of explosives in a variety of environments and at distances up to 100 m.
